Let’s dive into Chapter 6: Ambition and Stretch — Using OKRs to Drive Innovation.
One of the things that really sets the OKR framework apart is how it embraces ambition — what you might hear called “stretch goals.” Now, unlike the usual targets that feel safe and achievable, OKRs actually invite you and your team to reach just beyond what’s comfortable.
But let’s be clear. This isn’t about setting people up to fail. It’s about building an environment where bold ideas and innovation aren’t just allowed — they’re expected.
Think of stretch like a gentle nudge outside your comfort zone. Picture a runner who always keeps the same pace. Sure, it’s familiar, but growth? It’s not really happening. Now, imagine if that runner aims just a little higher, maybe tries for a faster time. Suddenly, they’re finding new energy and abilities they didn’t know were there.
That’s exactly how stretch OKRs work in organizations. They challenge teams to ask, “What’s truly possible here?” — not just, “What’s most likely?”
So, how do you make this work in real life? The OKR system actually splits goals into two categories.
First, you’ve got committed OKRs. These are the must-haves — realistic, but still challenging, and usually tied closely to the heart of your business.
Then there are aspirational OKRs. These are your big, bold “moonshot” goals. They might be out of reach, and that’s okay! The point is to push boundaries and spark new ways of thinking.
Here’s a quick example. Let’s say there’s a software company. Their committed OKR could sound like: “Reduce system downtime to less than zero point one percent.” That one? Non-negotiable. But at the same time, they set an aspirational OKR: “Double the user base in one year.”
The first is about what absolutely must get done. The second? That’s the stretch — it encourages the team to experiment, take risks, and maybe find new paths they hadn’t considered.
Why are these stretch OKRs so valuable?
Well, for starters, they help foster a growth mindset. Teams begin to see setbacks not as failures, but as chances to learn and adapt.
They also encourage experimentation. When the bar’s set high, you’re more likely to try something new — and maybe stumble onto a game-changing idea.
And, maybe most exciting, ambitious goals have a way of revealing hidden strengths and abilities that might have stayed beneath the surface otherwise.
Now, here’s something to pay attention to: it’s all about balance. If every single OKR is a stretch, people can get discouraged. The trick is to blend those committed goals with just enough aspiration — and to celebrate the progress, even if you don’t cross every finish line.
Let me share a real-world story. A global retailer once set an aspirational OKR: “Achieve carbon neutrality in all operations within five years.” They didn’t hit the goal completely, but the journey led to huge gains in energy efficiency, supply chain transparency, and employee engagement. All things that probably wouldn’t have happened with a safer, smaller target.
So, here’s the key takeaway. Stretch OKRs aren’t about being perfect. They’re about making progress, and building a culture where aiming high is simply part of who you are — a place where innovation isn’t the exception, it’s the habit you and your team share.
